text:
Protection de la jeunesse —
26160

2026 QCCS 262

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

TERREBONNE

No.:

700-24-000094-255

700-24-000096-250

DATE:

January 19
th
,
2026

_____________________________________________________________________

PRESIDED BY THE HONOURABLE AUDREY
BOCTOR, J.S.C
.

_____________________________________________________________________

A

B

Plaintiffs

v.

COURT OF QUEBEC,
Youth Protection Division for the Judicial
District A, to the attention of Justice Robert Proulx

Defendant

-and-

X

Impleaded Youth

-and-

[SOCIAL WORKER 1]
and
[SOCIAL WORKER 2]
in their capacity as designees of
the DIRECTOR OF YOUTH PROTECTION

Impleaded Director
of Youth Protection

-and-

ATTORNEY GENERAL OF
QUEBEC

Impleaded
Party

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT ON APPLICATION FOR
A STAY OF PROCEEDINGS (reCTIFIED)

_____________________________________________________________________

JB 6136

I.

OVERVIEW
[1]

[
1
]

The parties are currently involved in
proceedings before the Court of Quebec under the
Youth Protection Act
.
[2]
The proceedings stem from Motions
for Protection instituted in October 2021 and involve several families who are members
of the [Community A], an Orthodox Jewish community in Town A.

[
2
]

The parents have filed two applications for
judicial review of decisions rendered in the course of the proceedings. The
parents seek a stay of the proceedings before the Court of Quebec pending
adjudication of their applications for judicial review. The applications have
been joined together for a single hearing March
25-27
, 2026.

[
3
]

While the Court would not have granted a stay of
proceedings based on the first application for judicial review, the Court is of
the view that the circumstances of the second judicial review warrant granting
a partial suspension of pending proceedings until the Court renders its
decision.

II.

CONTEXT AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

[
4
]

A review of the relevant context and procedural
history is in order.

[
5
]

The Motions for Protection filed in October 2021
initially involved 135 youth.
[3]

The Motions for Protection allege that the security or development of the children
is in danger due to educational neglect, meaning a failure of the parental
environment to take the means to ensure that the child receives an adequate
education.

[
6
]

As explained in the motions, the youth in the
community attend religious schools that do not hold permits from the Quebec
Ministry of Education.
[4]

The Director of Youth Protection (“
DYP
”) alleges that, following
discussions with the families and religious authorities, a decision was made to
register the youth for home schooling, so as to enable the families to pursue
their religious lifestyle and to regulate the situation under the
Education
Act
.
[5]

[
7
]

The parents allege that they advised the
Ministry of Education in September 2020 that they are homeschooling parents, in
accordance with section 15(4)(a) of the
Education Act
.

[6]
According to the parents, they
have never received from the Ministry of Education or the DYP the detailed
requirements with which they must comply to have their learning project
approved.
[7]

The parents are of the view that the proceedings are an attack on their
religious freedom and that they are inadmissible and manifestly ill-founded, as
they are based solely on lack of compliance with the
Education Act
and
not on any actual inadequacy of the content of the education the youth are
receiving.

[
8
]

At the outset of the litigation, the parents
chose to be jointly represented by Me Anne-France Goldwater. Me Goldwater
ceased representing the parents for a brief period, between August and November
2024.
[8]

[
9
]

On behalf of the parents, Me Goldwater filed
several interlocutory motions before the Court of Quebec, including:

(i)

Application to disqualify a child’s advocate,
dated July 18, 2023, seeking to disqualify counsel designated by legal aid and put
a process in place to ensure that counsel appointed to represent the children
be able to communicate with them directly without a translator, and be
sufficiently apprised of the cultural, religious and educational requirements
of the community;
[9]

(ii)

Application to dismiss, dated September 29, 2023,
seeking to have the proceedings dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over the
subject-matter on the grounds that failure to meet the requirements of the
Education
Act
was not sufficient to constitute a situation compromising the security
of a child under the
Youth Protection Act
;
[10]

(iii)

An application alleging nullity of service of
the proceedings dated February 1, 2024, alleging that the proceedings were
never served properly on the parents or children, as required by section 76(1)
of the
Youth Protection

Act
;
[11]

(iv)

Application for change of venue dated April 5,
2024, alleging that the Courthouse A was unable to meet the parents’ needs and
seeking a transfer of the proceedings to Town B;
[12]

[
10
]

At a hearing held on September 18, 2025, Justice
Leroux dismissed the Application for change of venue, with written reasons to
follow.
[13]

The parents allege that the September 18, 2025, hearing had only been set
pro
forma
, to assess, further to Me Goldwater’s notice to cease
representing, whether the parents had appointed new counsel or decided to
represent themselves.
[14]

[
11
]

At the same hearing, Justice Leroux decided that
the remaining interlocutory applications, i.e. to contest service, disqualify
counsel and dismiss the proceedings, would be adjudicated October 28-31, 2024.
Justice Leroux ordered the DYP to serve the parents with notices of the
hearing.
[15]

[
12
]

The parents allege that the Notices of Presentation
dated October 15, 2024, were not served within the required time, were served
during the Jewish High Holidays, and were in some cases left outside and later
strewn about the neighbourhood. In any case, the Notices of Presentation did
not indicate what was proceeding, identifying only the DYP’s original Motion
for Protection.
[16]

[
13
]

Four parents attended the hearing on October 28,
2024. The parents allege that one of the parents, Rabbi C, held a mandate to
represent all the parents.  C requested a postponement of the hearing, which
Justice Leroux denied. Justice Leroux then dismissed all the pending procedural
motions orally, the reason recorded in the minutes being that the motions, on
their face, had no reasonable chance of success.
[17]

[
14
]

At the same hearing, and given that counsel
previously designated to represent certain youth had ceased representing in
October 2023, Justice Leroux appointed counsel to represent all the youth,
pursuant to section 78 YPA and article 160 C.C.P. Justice Leroux appointed Me
Michaël Pereira to represent the boys age 14 and over,
Me Julie Hamelin to represent the girls age 14 and
over, Me Patrick Cormier to represent the boys under age 14 and Me Nadia
Jamieson to represent the girls under age 14.
[18]

[
15
]

Me Goldwater resumed representing the parents
thereafter and attended a hearing on November 14, 2024.
[19]
At the hearing, she was
informed that the interlocutory motions had been dismissed but no written reasons
had yet been received.

[
16
]

The written judgment dismissing the application
to dismiss was signed on December 16, 2024.
[20]

The written judgments dismissing the application to disqualify, to nullify
service, and designating attorneys for the children were signed on December 23,
2024.
[21]

The parents allege that Me Goldwater received these judgments on January 10,
2025. On January 20, 2025, the parents filed an application to revoke the
judgments dismissing their interlocutory motions, rendered while they were not
represented by counsel alleging, among other things, that the parents had not
received proper notice of the hearing (“
Application in revocation
”)
[22]
.

[
17
]

A hearing on the Application in revocation was
held before Justice Proulx on February 10, 2025, and continued on March 11,
2025.
[23]

On March 24 2025, Justice Proulx dismissed an application to re-open the
hearing.
[24]

On March 26, 2025, Justice Proulx dismissed the Application in revocation on
the grounds that it was time-barred, having been filed outside the strict
30-day time limit which he held began to run on November 14, 2024.
[25]
Justice Proulx’s written
reasons were communicated on July 7, 2025.
[26]

[
18
]

On April 25, 2025, the parents filed an application
seeking judicial review of Justice Proulx’s decisions refusing to reopen the
hearing and dismissing their Application in revocation. The application also
seeks a stay of proceedings before the Court of Quebec pending adjudication
(the “
First Judicial Review
”).
[27]

[
19
]

The DYP filed an application to dismiss the
First Judicial Review on June 27, 2025.
[28]

The DYP’s application to dismiss was deferred to the merits by Justice Poisson
on July 17, 2025.
[29]

[
20
]

Meanwhile, on February 7, 2025, the parents had
also filed a notice to the Attorney General of Quebec (“
AGQ
”) pursuant
to Article 76 C.p.c. challenging the constitutionality of certain provisions of
the YPA and C.C.P. (the “
Notice
”).
[30]

The AGQ filed an application to dismiss the Notice on March 7, 2025,
[31]
including on grounds that it
constituted an abuse of process. Justice Proulx heard the AGQ’s Motion to
Dismiss on April 10, 2025.

[
21
]

On August 21, 2025, Justice Proulx informed the
parents that he was raising issues of abuse of process on his own motion.
[32]
The parents responded on
August 28, 2025, with a letter seeking clarifications including as to the
nature of the abuse being raised, to which Justice Proulx did not respond. On
September 3, 2025, Justice Proulx rendered judgment dismissing the Notice as
being abusive, and ordering that any further preliminary motions filed by the
parents and their counsel must first be submitted to him for a preliminary
screening to determine if they constitute an abuse of process.
[33]

[
22
]

On October 3, 2025, the parents filed an application
seeking judicial review of Justice Proulx’s decision dismissing the Notice and
seeking a stay of proceedings before the Court of Quebec pending adjudication
(the “
Second Judicial Review
”).
[34]

[
23
]

On October 30, 2025, the undersigned was designated
to case manage both the First and Second Judicial Reviews, to hear any
incidental applications, and to hear the applications on the merits.
[35]

[
24
]

On December 1, 2025, the AGQ filed an
application to dismiss the Second Judicial Review alleging that a judicial
review is not an available procedure and that the Second Judicial Review is
abusive.
[36]

[
25
]

On December 2, 2025, the Court heard the parents’
application for a stay of proceedings. The Court also asked the parties to
collaborate to identify dates to proceed promptly on the merits of the First
and Second Judicial Reviews.

[
26
]

The AGQ did not participate in the hearing on
the application for a stay of proceedings. The AGQ confirmed in written
correspondence that, provided the Applications for Judicial Review could be
heard promptly, the AGQ consented to defer its application to dismiss the
Second Judicial Review to the merits.

[
27
]

On December 11, 2025, the Court set the hearing
on the parents’ Applications for Judicial Review and the DYP and AGQ’s
Applications to Dismiss for March
25-27
, 2026.
[37]

[
28
]

There are currently two interlocutory
applications pending before the Court of Quebec. The first is an application by
Me Hamelin, counsel to the girls age 14 and over, to facilitate access to her
clients.
[38]

That application is to be heard on January 22, 2026.
[39]
The second is the parents’
Motion to lift
in camera
hearings dated March 21, 2025, which has not
been scheduled. Trial dates have not yet been set.

[
29
]

In the context of the First Judicial Review, Me
Goldwater, Me Pereira, Me Hamelin, Me Allard and Me Cormier had previously
agreed that the trial in first instance could not be set until final
adjudication on the application for judicial review.
[40]
The DYP has always noted its
disagreement with this position and its intention to contest any motion for a
stay of proceedings, but agreed not to raise the lateness of any such
application.

[
30
]

That said, at the hearing, Me Hamelin, Me Allard
and Me Cormier took the position that a stay should not be granted at this
time. Me Pereira supported the parents’ application for a stay of proceedings.

III.

APPLICABLE PRINCIPLES

[
31
]

Article 530 C.C.P. provides that an application
for judicial review does not stay proceedings pending before another court or
tribunal, or
the execution of the judgment or
decision under review, unless the court orders otherwise.
A stay is a
discretionary and exceptional remedy.
[41]

[
32
]

The criteria
for the issuance of a stay are well-established. The party seeking the stay
must demonstrate:

a)

an
appearance of right or serious issue to be tried in the underlying judicial
review proceedings;

b)

that the party will suffer serious or
irreparable harm if the stay is not granted;

c)

that the balance of convenience favours the issuance of the stay.
[42]

[
33
]

The court must examine the criteria as a
whole, each in relation to the other.
[43]
Each
criterion must be satisfied.
[44]

IV.

ANALYSIS

1.

Appearance of Right or serious issue to be tried

[
34
]

T
he
appearance of right is based on a preliminary assessment of the merits. The
Supreme Court has characterized this test as being undemanding and essentially
intended to exclude frivolous or vexatious remedies: “Once satisfied that the
application is neither vexatious nor frivolous, the motions judge should
proceed

to consider the second
and third tests, even if

of

the
opinion that the plaintiff is unlikely to succeed at trial. A prolonged
examination

of

the merits is generally neither
necessary nor desirable.”
[45]

[
35
]

Another way

of

defining this test is the serious
question to be tried. This is no different than the test

of

“appearance

of

right” and does not require a distinct
approach.
[46]

As the Supreme Court has explained, “[t]here are no specific requirements which
must be met in order to satisfy this test. The threshold is a low one. The
judge on the application must make a preliminary assessment

of

the merits

of

the case.”
[47]

[
36
]

While this hurdle is not onerous, it must be
satisfied. In addition, because the criteria must be weighed each in relation
to the other, the relative strengths of the parties’ positions can have an
impact at later stages of the analysis.
[48]

[
37
]

In this case, the Court must
examine the appearance of right in relation to each application for judicial
review.

a)

Appearance of Right
on the First Judicial Review

[
38
]

It is not contested that the First Judicial
Review seeks the review of interlocutory decisions, i.e. Justice Proulx’s
decisions (i) refusing to reopen the hearing on the application for revocation,
and (ii) dismissing the application for revocation as being time-barred.

[
39
]

The judicial review of interlocutory decisions
attracts heightened scrutiny. In
Société des casinos
, the Court of
Appeal reiterated that it is preferable not to seek judicial review of
interlocutory decisions and to instead let the matter run its course,
particularly in matters of proof and procedure. If necessary, the dissatisfied
party can seek judicial review once the final decision has been rendered.
[49]

[
40
]

These principles apply with at least the same
rigour in the context of youth protection proceedings, where interlocutory
decisions are not subject to appeal.
[50]

[
41
]

Exceptions to the rule are few and are to be
interpreted strictly.
[51]

Judicial review of an interlocutory decision may be justified where (i) the
interlocutory decision has important and irremediable consequences, notably in
cases of a serious breach of natural justice; (ii) the proceedings before the
decision-maker are clearly inadmissible; or (iii) the interlocutory decision
determines an issue of fundamental rights that the legislator did not intend to
confide to the decision-maker.
[52]

[
42
]

Finally,
in considering the appearance of right on the merits of the application for
judicial review, the Court must consider the standard of review applicable to
the impugned decision.

[
43
]

Based on a preliminary assessment of the merits,
the Court concludes that the First Judicial Review does not raise a serious
issue to be tried with respect to Justice Proulx’s refusal to reopen the
hearing. Justice Proulx was of the view that the timeliness of the application
in revocation was to be decided first, and it appears that the evidence the
Parents sought to submit did not relate to this issue.
[53]
At this stage, the Parents have
not demonstrated a serious issue to be tried on this aspect.

[
44
]

With respect to Justice Proulx’s decision to
dismiss the Application in revocation as being time-barred, the main issue is
his conclusion that counsel had sufficient notice of the judgments rendered as
of November 14, 2024, such that the parents’ strict 30-day time limit began to
run as of that date.

[
45
]

The standard of review applicable to this
determination appears to be that of reasonableness.
[54]
While counsel alleges having
been taken by surprise by this issue,  based on a
prima facie
review of
the file and the excerpts of the hearing provided, that argument does not
appear to be serious.
[55]

[
46
]

That said, while the parents have a steep hill
to climb, the Court cannot conclude that the remainder of the application is
frivolous or vexatious. While it is true that the case law does not require
detailed understanding of the judgment for the clock to start running under
article 347 C.C.P, the authorities relied upon by the DYP also indicate that
the 30-day period is meant to permit the party to have the judgment in hand and
to make an informed decision:

[81] L’argument
des défenderesses ne semble pas tenir compte du fait que le délai de 30 jours
vise à permettre au débiteur d’avoir le jugement en main, d’en prendre connaissance
en détail, de consulter un(e) avocat(e) s’il le veut et de prendre une décision
quant à la stratégie à adopter.
[56]

[
47
]

In the present case, the parents allege having
taken several actions, with great persistence, to obtain the recordings, minutes
of the hearing and the judgments.
[57]

Justice Proulx’s decision does not appear to engage with the parents’ argument
that the full written reasons for the judgments rendered orally on October 28,
2025, were only signed on December 16 and 23, respectively.

[
48
]

The Court notes that the parents have an
additional hurdle with respect to the judgment dismissing the parents’
application for change of venue. The parents allege that counsel received the
French-language version of the judgment on November 18
th
and 25
th
,
[58]
but that counsel received the
English-language version on January 10, 2025.
[59]

[
49
]

Finally, the decision to dismiss the Application
in revocation as being time-barred does appear, on a
prima facie
review
of the file, to involve significant and irremediable consequences for the
parents. While the DYP argues that the parents can still raise defects with
respect to the service of the proceedings on the merits, no party takes that
position with respect to any of the other issues raised in the preliminary
motions.

b)

Appearance of Right
on the Second Judicial Review

[
50
]

The Second Judicial Review concerns Justice
Proulx’s judgment dismissing the parents’ Notice pursuant to article 76 C.C.P.
and imposing a sanction for abuse of process.

[
51
]

However, while the Second Judicial Review
formally grants the AGQ’s application to dismiss in its conclusions, the
decision is based on considerations other than those raised by the AGQ:

Question en litige:

[6] Au moment de la prise en délibéré, le Tribunal considère que la
question en litige est de déterminer si la demande en rejet de l’avis
d’inconstitutionnalité doit être accueillie pour les motifs soulevés par le
PGQ.

[7]
Le Tribunal n'entend pas répondre à la question en litige
telle qu'elle s'est posée au départ
,
car il conclut d'office
que
l'avis d'inconstitutionnalité doit être analysé sous l'angle de l'abus de
procédure en application de l'article 51 C.p.c., à savoir
est-ce qu'il
constitue un abus en raison de l'utilisation excessive de la procédure par la
procureure des parents
, et par conséquent, des parents, parties au litige.

[Underlining added]

[
52
]

As noted above, Justice Proulx wrote to counsel
for the parents on August 21, 2025, and informed her that he was raising the
issue of abuse of process on his own motion, and that she had until September
1, 2025, to make representations to demonstrate that this was not the case.
[60]
The letter states as follows:

[
53
]

Counsel for the parents replied by letter on
August 28, 2025. She stated her view that the debate could not be re-opened and
asked for clarifications to allow her to respond, notably regarding the nature
of the abuse being raised, and the proceedings in relation to which abuse was
being raised. She also asked if the Court had considered whether a hearing was
required.
[61]

[
54
]

Justice Proulx rendered his judgment on
September 3, 2025, in which he indicated that he did not intend to respond to
counsel’s letter.
[62]

[
55
]

It appears from the judgment that Justice Proulx
considered the procedural motions to be abusive in their entirety.  After a detailed
review of the steps taken in the litigation to date and the delays incurred, he
concluded:

[96] Pour tous
ces motifs, the Tribunal considère que
les demandes interlocutoires

introduites
par l’avocate des parents sont injustifiées en ce qu’elles ne respectent pas le
principe de la proportionnalité
. Aussi, le Tribunal conclut que l’avocate
des parents a exercé la procédure de manière excessive et déraisonnable et
accorde la demande en rejet.

[97] En raison
de cette conclusion,
le Tribunal n’entend pas traiter des autres questions
soulevées par la demande en rejet
.

[98]
Aussi,
toutes nouvelles procédures introduites par les parents ou leur avocate devront
faire l’objet d’une évaluation préalable par le Tribunal afin de déterminer si
elles constituent un exercice abusif de la procédure retardant indûment le
traitement des demandes de la Directrice

[63]

[
56
]

The Court of Appeal recently reiterated that,
while abuse of process can undoubtedly be raised on a judge’s own motion, the
principles of procedural fairness must be respected:

[23]      Il n’est pas contesté que le juge pouvait soulever
d’office le caractère abusif de la conduite de l’une ou l’autre ou des deux
parties conformément à l’article 51 du
Code de procédure civile
.
Il
demeure qu’au terme du principe
audi alteram partem
, il revenait au juge
de communiquer son intention aux parties afin qu’elles puissent faire valoir
leurs arguments tant sur l’existence de l’abus que sur la sanction à celui-ci
.
Ce seul motif suffit pour intervenir sans qu’il soit nécessaire de se prononcer
tant sur le bienfondé des constats factuels du juge que sur la question [...]
[64]

[
57
]

Based on a
prima facie
review of the
file, the Court concludes that there is a serious issue to be tried as to
whether Justice Proulx’s letter gave the parents and their counsel adequate
notice of the nature of the abuse being raised on the judge’s own motion, and
the nature of the sanction he was therefore considering imposing, when the
AGQ’s application was focussed on the Notice and sought to have it dismissed on
different grounds than those retained by the judge.  There is also a serious
issue as to whether the parents and their counsel were afforded an appropriate
opportunity to respond in the circumstances.

[
58
]

The Court can certainly understand that counsel’s
letter went beyond what was necessary to seek clarifications. However, the
issue remains the adequacy of Justice Proulx’s letter.

[
59
]

The Court notes that the DYP also invited the
Court to consider certain arguments raised by the AGQ in its application to
dismiss the Second Judicial Review, acknowledging however that these issues
could not be fully adjudicated in the AGQ’s absence. Essentially, the AGQ
alleges that, because the judgment dismissing the Notice puts an end to the
proceedings against the AGQ, the judgment is not subject to judicial review but
rather to leave to appeal pursuant to article 30, paragraph 2(5) C.C.P. The DYP
further raises the applicability of section 100 of the YPA, which would have
required the parents to file an appeal and not a judicial review.

[
60
]

The Court agrees that these are serious
arguments that will need to be fully debated at the upcoming hearing in March.
However, they do not defeat the parents’ appearance of right at this
prima
facie
stage.

2.

serious or irreparable prejudice

[
61
]

With respect to the Second Judicial Review, the
Court concludes that this criterion is satisfied.

[
62
]

The parents have demonstrated, on a
prima
facie
basis, a relatively strong appearance of right on a question of
procedural fairness in the context of a judgment that considers all their
procedural motions to have been abusive. This weighs in the analysis
[65]
.

[
63
]

While no one can fault Justice Proulx for
seeking to move these proceedings towards a hearing on the merits, if the
parents succeed on their Second Judicial Review, there is a very strong
argument that the appropriate remedy is to quash the decision and remit the
AGQ’s application to dismiss the Notice to the Court of Quebec, regardless of
whether the reviewing court agrees with the decision in whole or in part :

[…] the denial of a right to a fair
hearing must always render a decision invalid, whether or not it may appear to
a reviewing court that the hearing would likely have resulted in a different
decision. The right to a fair hearing must be regarded as an independent,
unqualified right which finds its essential justification in the sense of
procedural justice which any person affected by an administrative decision is
entitled to have. It is not for a court to deny that right and sense of justice
on the basis of speculation as to what the result might have been had there
been a hearing.
[66]

[
64
]

In addition, where the decision-maker has
expressed a view on the outcome of the proceeding to be remitted, the usual
remedy is to send the matter to another decision-maker.
[67]

[
65
]

The next step in the proceedings is an
application by Me Hamelin seeking an order to compel the parents to cooperate
to facilitate her access to the youth she was appointed to represent, the girls
age 14 and over. At the hearing, Me Hamelin argued that the parents could still
oppose her application and raise the same arguments they raised in the
application to disqualify counsel. Setting aside that the application to
disqualify was dismissed by Justice Leroux and is one of the judgments wrapped
up in the First Judicial Review, on a more basic level, the judgment being
challenged on the Second Judicial Review already considers that the application
to disqualify is abusive. The same can be inferred regarding the parents’
application to lift the
in camera
hearings.

[
66
]

Proceeding in these circumstances is clearly
prejudicial to the parents. A judgment has been rendered that not only considers
all the prior motions to have been abusive, but that is also intended to have
an important impact on the conduct of the proceedings going forward through the
sanction imposed. If the parents succeed on the Second Judicial Review, quashing
and remitting the decision will not remedy the prejudice suffered in the
meantime.

[
67
]

The suggestion that the parents can simply bring
another application for judicial review in the event they are dissatisfied with
the decision on Me Hamelin’s motion is not conducive to a prompt resolution of
the judicial review applications in the best interests of all concerned.

3.

Balance of Convenience

[
68
]

At this stage, the Court must consider which of
the parties will suffer the greater prejudice if the stay is not granted,
taking into account the public interest.
[68]

[
69
]

The Court is alive to the context of these proceedings.
The courts
, like the representatives of the youth
protection directors, must make decisions that are “in the interest of the
child and respect his rights”.
[69]

In addition, the impact of the passage of time is not the same for youth
as for adults. Youth protection matters are meant to proceed diligently to
redress situations that are alleged to compromise a child’s development and
security. For this reason, the matter is under special case management and the
proceedings were prioritized such that both motions to dismiss and both
judicial reviews are being heard March
25-27
, 2026.

[
70
]

The parents take a no holds barred approach to
this litigation in a context where they perceive the survival of their
community and way of life to be under threat. There is no doubt that this
causes friction with the purposes of the
Youth Protection Act
. At the
same time, these are not usual youth protection proceedings. Usually, “
the tribunal is called upon to render justice in an individualized
and particularized manner on the basis of a single child’s situation
.”
[70]
These proceedings, initially involving 135 youth,
and raising complex issues of religious freedom, challenge the usual way of
proceeding.

[
71
]

The Court notes that while the Motions for
Protection were filed in October 2021, they were postponed
sine die
for
approximately one year between February 23, 2022, and March 29, 2023, to allow
the parties to pursue an out-of-court resolution
[71]
. The DYP amended its
proceedings on March 13, 2023, to seek interim relief,
[72]
but Justice Leroux dismissed
the request on the grounds that the amended motion contained no facts alleging
the need for urgent intervention. Justice Leroux invited the DYP to return in
the coming days or weeks with a “proper motion” to support the request for
interim relief, but the DYP did not do so.
[73]

[
72
]

While there is undoubtedly an interest for the
youth concerned, as well as all parties and the public, in ensuring that youth
protection matters proceed with celerity, there is also a public interest in
ensuring that the proceedings are fair. These proceedings involve a community
that already has limited contact with public institutions. It is in the best
interests of all concerned, and most importantly the youth, that the proceedings
not only be fair, but that they be perceived to be fair.

[
73
]

In the exceptional circumstances of this case,
and weighing all the factors together, the Court concludes that the balance of
convenience favours granting the application, in part.

[
74
]

Given the context, the Court will not grant a
blanket stay of proceedings as sought. Youth protection is an evolving
landscape. Just as a situation may evolve towards a resolution,
[74]
a situation may also
deteriorate requiring intervention. A total stay of proceedings is not
appropriate. The Court will order that the pending steps identified by the
parties, namely the Application to Order Measures Aimed at Ensuring Compliance
with Section 78 of the Y.P.A. dated April 8, 2025, the Motion to lift
in
camera
hearings dated March 21, 2025, and the trials on the merits in all
files joined pursuant to the order rendered by the Court of Quebec on March 11,
2025, proceed only after this Court renders its decision.
[75]

FOR
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
75
]

GRANTS
, in part,
the parents’ application for a stay of proceedings;

[
76
]

that the

to Order Measures Aimed at Ensuring Compliance with Section 78 of the Y.P.A
.
